title: Neutralisation and salts; Oxidation states and naming
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: RX02#t3 term and clue written for the game; RX02#t2 term and clue written for the game; RX02#t1 term and clue written for the game; AB04#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB04#N.4, RX02#N.4a, AB04#N.10, RX02#N.8, AB04#N.15, RX02#N.9, RX02#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Metal hydride
items.clue: Compound such as NaH or CaH₂ in which H is −1.

items.label: Peroxide
items.clue: Compound such as H₂O₂ or Na₂O₂ in which O is −1.

items.label: Oxidation number
items.clue: The charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic.

items.label: Parent acid
items.clue: The neutral compound that supplies the anion of a salt, e.g. HNO₃ for KNO₃.

questions.stem: Which reaction produces a salt and water, with no other product?
questions.explanation: Each OH⁻ takes one H⁺ to form water: Ba(OH)₂ + 2HNO₃ → Ba(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O.

questions.stem: What are the oxidation numbers of hydrogen in sodium hydride, NaH, and of oxygen in sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂?
questions.explanation: In NaH, Na is +1, so H is −1 (the hydride ion). In Na₂O₂, 2(+1) + 2x = 0, so O is −1 (the peroxide ion, O₂²⁻).

questions.stem: What are the parent acid and parent base of ammonium methanoate, HCOONH₄?

options.text: Parent acid HCOO⁻; parent base NH₄⁺
Parent acid HCOOH; parent base NH₄⁺
Parent acid NH₃; parent base HCOOH
Parent acid HCOOH; parent base NH₃

questions.explanation: The anion HCOO⁻ comes from methanoic acid; the cation NH₄⁺ formed when NH₃ accepted a proton. HCOOH + NH₃ → HCOONH₄.
2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 gives 2x = +12, so each Cr is +6. The numeral is per atom.

questions.stem: Baking powder contains sodium hydrogencarbonate and a solid acid. When the cake batter gets wet, the two react. Why does the cake rise?

options.text: HCO₃⁻ accepts H⁺ from the acid, giving water and carbon dioxide gas.
The acid reacts with sodium, giving hydrogen gas.
A salt and water form, as in every neutralisation, and the steam lifts the cake.
HCO₃⁻ donates H⁺ to the acid, giving CO₃²⁻ and a gas.

questions.explanation: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂. The bubbles of CO₂ make the batter rise, just as CO₂ from a carbonate antacid makes you burp.

questions.stem: What is the formula of sodium chlorate(III)?
questions.explanation: In ClO₂⁻, x + 2(−2) = −1, so Cl = +3. One Na⁺ balances the 1− charge.

questions.stem: Chlorine is −1 in the chloride ion, Cl⁻, but +1 in the hypochlorite ion, ClO⁻ (in bleach). Which explains the +1?

options.text: The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ has lost a proton to the oxygen atom, leaving chlorine with a +1 charge.
Oxygen always has the oxidation number −1 in an ion with one negative charge.
Oxygen is more electronegative than chlorine, so it is assigned the shared electrons in the Cl–O bond.
The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ carries a real charge of +1, as in a Cl⁺ ion.

questions.explanation: O takes both shared electrons and is −2; the total must be −1, so x + (−2) = −1 and Cl is +1. In Cl⁻, chlorine holds an extra electron: −1.
